paragraphs: Agriculture is perhaps, of all the useful arts, the one that improves most slowly among democratic nations. Often it even seems to stand still, because other arts are advancing rapidly toward perfection. On the other hand, almost all the tastes and habits that equality of conditions produces naturally lead men to commercial and industrial occupations.

Suppose an active, educated, and free man who has a comfortable competence but is full of desires. He is too poor to live in idleness, yet rich enough to feel protected from the immediate fear of want, and he wonders how he can better his condition. This man has acquired a taste for physical gratifications, in which thousands of his fellow men indulge around him. He has begun to enjoy these pleasures himself, and he is eager to increase his means of satisfying these tastes more fully. But life is slipping away and time presses. What is he to turn to? Cultivating the ground promises an almost certain result for his efforts, but a slow one; men do not grow rich by it without patience and toil. Agriculture is therefore suited only to those who already have large, superfluous wealth, or to those whose poverty bids them seek only a bare subsistence. The choice of a man such as we have supposed is soon made. He sells his plot of ground, leaves his dwelling, and embarks on some hazardous but lucrative calling. Democratic communities abound in men of this kind, and as equality of conditions grows, their number increases. Thus democracy not only swells the number of working men; it also leads them to prefer one kind of labor to another. While it turns them away from agriculture, it encourages their taste for commerce and manufactures. *a

[Footnote a: People have often remarked that manufacturers and merchants are excessively addicted to physical gratifications, and this has been attributed to commerce and manufactures. But I think that is to mistake the effect for the cause. Commerce and manufactures do not give men the taste for physical gratifications; rather, it is this taste that leads men into commerce and manufactures, as a means by which they hope to satisfy themselves more quickly and more fully. If commerce and manufactures increase the desire for well-being, it is because every passion gathers strength in proportion as it is cultivated, and grows with all the efforts made to satisfy it. All the causes that make the love of worldly welfare predominate in the heart of man are favorable to the growth of commerce and manufactures. Equality of conditions is one of those causes. It encourages trade, not directly by giving men a taste for business, but indirectly by strengthening and expanding in their minds a taste for prosperity.]

Even the wealthiest members of the community show this spirit. In a democratic country a man may be reckoned very rich, yet he is almost always dissatisfied with his fortune, since he sees that he has less than his father had and worries that his sons will have less than he does. So most rich men in democracies are tormented by the wish to gain still more wealth, and they turn naturally to trade and manufactures, which look like the quickest and strongest roads to success. In this they share the instincts of the poor without being under the same pressures. Or rather, they are under the most commanding pressure of all: the need not to slip down in the world.

In aristocracies, the rich are also the men who govern. The attention they ceaselessly give to important public affairs keeps them from the lesser cares that trade and manufactures demand. Suppose, nevertheless, that an individual’s own will turns his attention to business. The will of the body to which he belongs will immediately bar him from pursuing it. For however much men may rail against the rule of numbers, they cannot wholly escape its sway, and even among those aristocratic bodies that most obstinately refuse to acknowledge the rights of the majority of the nation, a private majority forms that governs the rest. *b

[Footnote b: Some aristocracies, however, have plunged eagerly into commerce and have developed manufactures with success. World history offers several striking examples. But in general one can say that the aristocratic principle does not favor the growth of trade and manufactures. Moneyed aristocracies are the only exception to this rule. In them, almost every desire needs wealth to be satisfied. The love of riches becomes, so to speak, the main highway of the human passions, and every lesser path crosses it or joins it. Love of money and thirst for the distinction that comes with power are then so closely mixed in the same souls that it is hard to tell whether men turn greedy out of ambition or ambitious out of greed. This is the case in England, where men try to get rich in order to gain distinction, and seek distinction as a way of displaying their wealth. The mind is then gripped from both ends and hurried into trade and manufactures, which are the shortest roads to opulence.

This, however, strikes me as an exceptional and transitory circumstance. When wealth has become the only symbol of aristocracy, it is very difficult for the wealthy to keep sole possession of political power to the exclusion of all other men. The aristocracy of birth and pure democracy stand at the two extremes of the social and political state of nations, and the moneyed aristocracy finds its place between them. It comes close to the aristocracy of birth by conferring great privileges on a small number of persons. It belongs to the democratic element in that these privileges may be acquired in turn by anyone. It often forms a natural transition between these two conditions of society, and it is hard to say whether it closes the reign of aristocratic institutions or already opens the new era of democracy.]

In democratic countries, money does not lead those who have it to political power, and often removes them from it. There the rich do not know how to spend their leisure. They are driven into active life by the restlessness and greatness of their desires, by the extent of their resources, and by the taste for the extraordinary that is almost always felt by those who rise above the crowd by whatever means. Trade is the only road open to them. In democracies nothing is greater or more brilliant than commerce. It attracts the attention of the public and fills the imagination of the multitude, and all energetic passions are directed toward it. Neither their own prejudices nor anyone else’s can keep the rich from devoting themselves to it. The wealthy members of democracies never form a body with customs and regulations of its own. The opinions peculiar to their class do not restrain them, and the common opinions of their country urge them on. Moreover, since all the large fortunes found in a democratic community have grown out of commerce, many generations must follow one another before their owners can entirely lay aside their habits of business.

Confined within the narrow space that politics leaves them, rich men in democracies throw themselves eagerly into commercial enterprise. There they can extend and use their natural advantages. Indeed, the boldness and scale of their industrial speculations let us measure how slight an esteem they would have had for productive industry if they had been born into an aristocracy.

A similar observation applies to all men living in democracies, whether poor or rich. Those who live amid democratic fluctuations always have the phantom of chance before their eyes, and they end by liking every undertaking in which chance plays a part. All of them are therefore led to engage in commerce, not only for the profit it holds out to them but for love of the constant excitement that this pursuit provides.

The United States of America has been free for only half a century [in 1840] from the colonial dependence in which it stood toward Great Britain. Large fortunes there are few, and capital is still scarce. Yet no people in the world has made such rapid progress in trade and manufactures as the Americans. Today they are the second maritime nation in the world, and although their manufactures must struggle against almost insurmountable natural obstacles, they are not prevented from making great advances every day. In the United States the greatest undertakings and speculations are carried out without difficulty, because the whole population is engaged in productive industry, and because the poorest members of the commonwealth, like the wealthiest, are ready to combine their efforts for such purposes. As a result, a stranger is constantly amazed by the immense public works carried out by a nation that contains, so to speak, no rich men. The Americans arrived on the territory they inhabit only yesterday, and they have already changed the whole order of nature to their own advantage. They have joined the Hudson to the Mississippi and linked the Atlantic Ocean with the Gulf of Mexico across a continent of more than five hundred leagues that separates the two seas. The longest railroads built up to the present time are in America. But what astonishes me most in the United States is not so much the marvelous grandeur of some undertakings as the innumerable multitude of small ones. Almost all the farmers of the United States combine some trade with agriculture, and most of them make agriculture itself a trade. It seldom happens that an American farmer settles for good on the land he occupies. Especially in the districts of the Far West, he brings land into tillage in order to sell it again, not to farm it. He builds a farmhouse on the speculation that, since the condition of the country will soon be changed by the growth of population, a good price will be had for it. Every year a swarm of inhabitants of the North arrives in the Southern States and settles where the cotton plant and the sugar cane grow. These men cultivate the soil to make it yield, in a few years, enough to enrich them, and they already look forward to the time when they can return home to enjoy the competence thus acquired. Thus the Americans carry their business-like qualities into agriculture, and their trading passions show there as in their other pursuits.

The Americans advance enormously in productive industry because every one of them throws himself into it at the same time. For that very reason they face unexpected and formidable troubles. Everyone is in commerce, so their commercial affairs depend on causes too varied and tangled for anyone to predict what trouble may come. Everyone is more or less in productive industry, so at the slightest jolt to business every private fortune is endangered at once, and the state itself is shaken. I believe that these recurring commercial panics are a disease native to the democratic nations of our age. It can be made less dangerous, but it cannot be cured, since it springs not from accidents but from the temperament of these nations.
